summary.text: For the error term \(J_n=B_n-eA_n\), polynomial integration identities show that \(J_{2k+1}=(-1)^k I_{k+1}\), where \(I_k=\frac1{k!}\int_0^1[x(1-x)]^k e^{1-x}\,dx\); the defining recurrences also give \(2J_{2k}=(2k+1)J_{2k-1}+J_{2k-3}\). Since \(0\le I_k\le e/k!\) (and hence both \(I_k\) and \(kI_k\) vanish), both parity subsequences of \(J_n\) tend to zero, while an induction gives \(A_n\ge1\), so division by \(A_n\) preserves the vanishing error.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a_n=A340738(n),\qquad b_n=A340737(n).
\]
Thus, apart from the irrelevant zeroth terms \(a_0=b_0=0\), the initial values are
\[
a_1=1,\quad a_2=2,\qquad b_1=3,\quad b_2=5,
\]
and both sequences obey the same parity-dependent recurrence. For odd \(n\ge 3\),
\[
s_n=2s_{n-1}+n s_{n-2},                                      \tag{1}
\]
while for even \(n\ge4\),
\[
s_n=\frac{n+2}{2}s_{n-1}-s_{n-2}-\frac{n-2}{2}s_{n-3}.       \tag{2}
\]
Here \(s\) may be either \(a\) or \(b\). In the original definition the subtraction in (2) is subtraction in the natural numbers, hence potentially truncated. We will first prove inequalities which show that all the later rearrangements of this recurrence are legitimate.

We write \(e=\exp(1)\). The goal is to prove
\[
\frac{b_n}{a_n}\longrightarrow e.
\]

## 1. Positivity and control of the natural-number subtraction

For either of the two sequences \(s=a,b\), and every \(k\ge1\), we claim
\[
\begin{aligned}
&1\le s_{2k-1},\qquad s_{2k-1}<s_{2k}<s_{2k+1},                 \tag{3}\\
&s_{2k}+k s_{2k-1}\le (k+1)s_{2k+1}.                          \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]

We prove these assertions simultaneously by induction on \(k\). For \(a\), the first three relevant values are
\[
a_1=1,\quad a_2=2,\quad a_3=2a_2+3a_1=7;
\]
for \(b\), they are
\[
b_1=3,\quad b_2=5,\quad b_3=2b_2+3b_1=19.
\]
Thus (3) and (4) hold at \(k=1\): respectively, \(2+1\le2\cdot7\) and \(5+3\le2\cdot19\).

Suppose they hold for some \(k\ge1\), and abbreviate
\[
x=s_{2k-1},\qquad y=s_{2k},\qquad z=s_{2k+1}.
\]
Then \(1\le x<y<z\). Since these are integers,
\[
y\le z-1,\qquad x\le z-2.
\]
The even recurrence defining the next term is
\[
s_{2k+2}=(k+2)z-y-kx,
\]
with natural-number subtraction. We have
\[
\begin{aligned}
y+kx+z
&\le (z-1)+k(z-2)+z\\
&=(k+2)z-(2k+1)\\
&<(k+2)z.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, the quantities subtracted do not exhaust \((k+2)z\), so the natural subtraction agrees with ordinary integer subtraction, and
\[
s_{2k+2}>z=s_{2k+1}.
\]
The next odd recurrence gives
\[
s_{2k+3}=2s_{2k+2}+(2k+3)s_{2k+1}>s_{2k+2}.
\]
It also gives the next instance of (4), since all terms are nonnegative and
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(k+2)s_{2k+3}-\bigl(s_{2k+2}+(k+1)s_{2k+1}\bigr)\\
&=(2k+3)s_{2k+2}
 +\bigl((k+2)(2k+3)-(k+1)\bigr)s_{2k+1}\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This completes the induction and proves (3)–(4) for both \(a\) and \(b\).

In particular, for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
a_n\ge1.                                                       \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, this follows directly from (3), according as \(n\) is odd or even.

For later use, we now rewrite the even recurrence without subtraction. For \(k\ge2\), (2) says
\[
s_{2k}=(k+1)s_{2k-1}-s_{2k-2}-(k-1)s_{2k-3}.                  \tag{6}
\]
By (4) with index \(k-1\),
\[
s_{2k-2}+(k-1)s_{2k-3}\le k s_{2k-1}\le(k+1)s_{2k-1}.
\]
Thus the subtractions in (6) are nontruncated, and we may rearrange it as
\[
s_{2k}+s_{2k-2}+(k-1)s_{2k-3}=(k+1)s_{2k-1}.                 \tag{7}
\]

## 2. Recurrences involving only odd-indexed terms

For \(k\ge2\), the odd recurrence at index \(2k-1\) is
\[
s_{2k-1}=2s_{2k-2}+(2k-1)s_{2k-3}.                           \tag{8}
\]
Combining (7) and (8) eliminates \(s_{2k-2}\). Multiplying (7) by \(2\), and observing from (8) that
\[
2s_{2k-2}+(2k-2)s_{2k-3}=s_{2k-1}-s_{2k-3},
\]
we obtain
\[
2s_{2k}=(2k+1)s_{2k-1}+s_{2k-3}.                              \tag{9}
\]
Now use the odd recurrence at index \(2k+1\):
\[
s_{2k+1}=2s_{2k}+(2k+1)s_{2k-1}.
\]
Substitution of (9) gives the pure odd-index recurrence
\[
s_{2k+1}=(4k+2)s_{2k-1}+s_{2k-3},\qquad k\ge2.               \tag{10}
\]
Equations (9) and (10) hold for both \(s=a\) and \(s=b\).

Define the linear error
\[
J_n=b_n-ea_n.
\]
Because the recurrences are linear, subtracting \(e\) times the recurrence for \(a\) from that for \(b\) yields, for \(k\ge2\),
\[
J_{2k+1}=(4k+2)J_{2k-1}+J_{2k-3},                             \tag{11}
\]
and
\[
2J_{2k}=(2k+1)J_{2k-1}+J_{2k-3}.                              \tag{12}
\]
We shall identify the odd errors exactly with a family of rapidly decreasing integrals.

## 3. A family of integrals and its recurrence

Put
\[
U(x)=x(1-x),\qquad P_k(x)=\frac{U(x)^k}{k!},
\]
and define
\[
I_k=\int_0^1 P_k(x)e^{1-x}\,dx
   =\int_0^1\frac{(x(1-x))^k}{k!}e^{1-x}\,dx.                 \tag{13}
\]
For \(k\ge1\), introduce the auxiliary polynomial
\[
G_k(x)=\frac{U(x)^k}{(k+1)!}
       \bigl(x^2+(2k+1)x-(k+1)\bigr).                         \tag{14}
\]
We claim the polynomial identity
\[
G_k'=P_{k+1}+(4k+2)P_k-P_{k-1}+G_k.                           \tag{15}
\]

Here is the calculation. Let
\[
H(x)=x^2+(2k+1)x-(k+1).
\]
Since \(U'=1-2x\) and \(H'=2x+2k+1\), multiplication of \(G_k'-G_k\) by \((k+1)!\), followed by factoring out \(U^{k-1}\), reduces (15) to
\[
kU'H+U(H'-H)
 =U^2+(4k+2)(k+1)U-k(k+1).                                   \tag{16}
\]
Substituting \(U=x-x^2\), \(U'=1-2x\), and the displayed expressions for \(H,H'\), both sides expand to the same polynomial. This proves (16), and hence (15); the factorial coefficients used here are simply
\[
\frac{(k+1)!}{k!}=k+1,
\qquad
\frac{(k+1)!}{(k-1)!}=k(k+1).
\]

We next use the elementary integration identity
\[
\int_0^1 (R-R')(x)e^{1-x}\,dx=R(0)e-R(1)                     \tag{17}
\]
valid for every polynomial \(R\). Indeed,
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(-R(x)e^{1-x}\bigr)=(R(x)-R'(x))e^{1-x},
\]
so (17) follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus.

For \(k\ge1\), the factor \(U^k\) in (14) shows that
\[
G_k(0)=G_k(1)=0.                                               \tag{18}
\]
Equation (15) says
\[
P_{k+1}+(4k+2)P_k-P_{k-1}=G_k'-G_k.
\]
The integral of the right side against \(e^{1-x}\) is zero: apply (17) to \(R=-G_k\), for which \(R-R'=G_k'-G_k\), and then use (18). Therefore
\[
I_{k+1}+(4k+2)I_k-I_{k-1}=0,
\]
or equivalently
\[
I_{k+1}=-(4k+2)I_k+I_{k-1},\qquad k\ge1.                     \tag{19}
\]

We also need the first two values. For \(I_1\), take
\[
R(x)=-x^2-x-1.
\]
Then
\[
R-R'=x-x^2=U=P_1,
\]
and (17), together with \(R(0)=-1\), \(R(1)=-3\), gives
\[
I_1=3-e.                                                       \tag{20}
\]
For \(I_2\), take
\[
Q(x)=\frac12x^4+x^3+\frac72x^2+7x+7.
\]
A direct differentiation gives
\[
Q-Q'=\frac12x^2(1-x)^2=P_2.
\]
Since \(Q(0)=7\) and \(Q(1)=19\), (17) gives
\[
I_2=7e-19.                                                     \tag{21}
\]

On the other hand, the initial odd errors are
\[
J_1=3-e=I_1,
\qquad
J_3=19-7e=-I_2.                                                \tag{22}
\]
We now prove, for every \(k\ge0\), the exact identity
\[
J_{2k+1}=(-1)^k I_{k+1}.                                      \tag{23}
\]
The cases \(k=0,1\) are precisely (22). Suppose \(k\ge2\) and that the formula is known for the two preceding odd indices. By (11),
\[
\begin{aligned}
J_{2k+1}
&=(4k+2)(-1)^{k-1}I_k+(-1)^{k-2}I_{k-1}\\
&=(-1)^k\bigl(-(4k+2)I_k+I_{k-1}\bigr)\\
&=(-1)^k I_{k+1},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality is (19). Thus (23) follows by induction.

## 4. Decay of the integrals and of all errors

For \(0\le x\le1\),
\[
0\le U(x)=x(1-x)\le1,
\qquad
0<e^{1-x}\le e.
\]
Consequently the integrand in (13) is nonnegative, and it is bounded above by \(e/k!\). Since the interval has length one,
\[
0\le I_k\le\frac{e}{k!}.                                     \tag{24}
\]
Because \(1/k!\to0\), the squeeze theorem gives
\[
I_k\longrightarrow0.                                         \tag{25}
\]
Equation (23) now implies immediately that
\[
J_{2k+1}\longrightarrow0.                                    \tag{26}
\]

To control the even errors through (12), we also need a linearly weighted version of (25). For \(k\ge1\),
\[
\frac{k}{k!}=\frac1{(k-1)!}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Multiplying (24) by \(k\ge0\) therefore yields
\[
0\le kI_k\le e\frac{k}{k!}\longrightarrow0,
\]
so
\[
kI_k\longrightarrow0.                                       \tag{27}
\]
For \(k\ge1\), (23) with index \(k-1\) gives
\[
J_{2k-1}=(-1)^{k-1}I_k.
\]
Hence
\[
\left|(2k+1)J_{2k-1}\right|
=(2k+1)I_k=2(kI_k)+I_k\longrightarrow0                       \tag{28}
\]
by (25) and (27). Also, (26) remains true after shifting the odd index, so
\[
J_{2k-3}\longrightarrow0.                                    \tag{29}
\]
Using (12), for \(k\ge2\),
\[
J_{2k}=\frac12\bigl((2k+1)J_{2k-1}+J_{2k-3}\bigr).
\]
Equations (28) and (29) show that
\[
J_{2k}\longrightarrow0.                                      \tag{30}
\]

Since both the even and odd subsequences tend to zero, the whole sequence does:
\[
J_n\longrightarrow0.                                         \tag{31}
\]
Explicitly, given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(N_0,N_1\) so that the even terms with half-index at least \(N_0\) and the odd terms with half-index at least \(N_1\) have absolute value less than \(\varepsilon\). Then every
\[
n\ge\max(2N_0,2N_1+1)
\]
is either \(2k\) with \(k\ge N_0\), or \(2k+1\) with \(k\ge N_1\), proving (31).

## 5. Passage from the linear error to the quotient

By (5), \(a_n\ge1\) for every \(n\ge1\). Thus \(a_n\ne0\) and
\[
0<\frac1{a_n}\le1.                                           \tag{32}
\]
For every \(n\ge1\),
\[
\frac{b_n}{a_n}-e
=\frac{b_n-ea_n}{a_n}
=\frac{J_n}{a_n}.                                              \tag{33}
\]
It follows from (32) that
\[
\left|\frac{b_n}{a_n}-e\right|
\le |J_n|.
\]
The right-hand side tends to zero by (31), so the squeeze theorem gives
\[
\frac{b_n}{a_n}-e\longrightarrow0.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{A340737(n)}{A340738(n)}\longrightarrow e}
\qquad(n\to\infty),
\]
as required.
